newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS-Austria's CA battle calms as decision nears.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Austria's CA battle calms as decision nears.

text.p: An eerie calm shrouded Europe's longest running privatisation battle on Friday as bidders took up their positions ahead of the final showdown in the sale of Austrian flagship bank Creditanstalt.

Finance Minister Viktor Klima, who had given suitors a deadline to improve their offers of 9 a.m. (0800 GMT), spent the day locked in his office with a gaggle of lawyers and financial advisers to ponder the updated bids.
Sources inside the ministry said a detailed evaluation of the offers, each believed to be accompanied by reams of legal documents, could take all weekend.

Klima earlier on Friday told Austrian state television he would announce the winner of the seven-year fight for control of Austria's number two bank before Tuesday, when parliament is due to hold a special session on the politically fraught sale.
Bank Austria, believed to lead the race, squeezed in its updated offer minutes before the deadline ran out.
"We've handed our improved offer to Klima just before 9 a.m.. I'm not allowed to say anything about its contents," a Bank Austria spokesman told Reuters.
The group originally bid 16.8 billion schillings ($1.52 billion) for the state's 70 percent voting stake in the bank, about 863 schillings a share and 16 percent above their market value.

Its closest rival, an international consortium of industrial and financial interests headed by Austro-Italian insurer EA-Generali, also bettered its existing offer of 13.8 billion schillings for the bank, but gave no details.

A maverick offer by former retail mogul Karl Wlaschek was the unknown third. No details of the multi-billionaire's bid have been released, but media reports have put the offer at around 15 billion schillings.
The sale of 141-year-old Creditanstalt has driven a wedge between Austria's coalition government partners, the Social Democrats (SPOe) and the conservative People's Party (OeVP).
The SPOe wants to see Creditanstalt sold to Bank Austria, which is effectively controlled by the Social Democrat-led City of Vienna council.
The OeVP, together with Creditanstalt's management, support the consortium to avoid a selloff of Austria's establishment bank to what they say is a "socialist" dinosaur bank.
In a last-ditch attempt to restore unity, senior leaders of the coalition parties agreed to hold an emergency session on Saturday to hammer out their differences.
Both camps on Friday appeared eager to tone down their political bickering, which has muddied the waters surrounding the seemingly endless privatisation project.
"Nobody, including the People's Party, is seriously questioning the coalition," Vranitzky told Austrian radio.

Conservative chief whip Andreas Khol said the coalition was suffering a crisis of confidence but he was sure it would pull through. "It's a serious illness, a crisis of trust...but we do not see the government collapsing," he told Reuters.

Sources close to the talks have put their money on Bank Austria emerging as the future owner of its main competitor, raising the prospect of a major shakeup of Austria's coveted and overcrowded financial sector.
With combined assets of 1,400 billion schillings and some 15,000 employees, the new bank would be a giant by Austrian standards and enter the league of Europe's top 30 banks. ($1=11.09 Schilling)
